edits.defect: Breadth-of-attribution overclaim: the section asserted that ALL FOUR commentaries supply an object for the messengers' despair and answer 'the same way'. Only three do. al-Jalalayn supplies no object at all.
edits.before:
The verse says that the messengers reached a point of despair, and it matters enormously **what** they despaired of. All four commentaries answer that question, and they answer it the same way.

Al-Tabari: until the messengers despaired *of their people believing them and accepting them as truthful*. Al-Muyassar: until they despaired *of their people's belief*. Ibn Kathir reports the same from Sa'id b. Jubayr, Ibn Mas'ud and Mujahid.
edits.after:
The verse says that the messengers reached a point of despair, and it matters enormously **what** they despaired of. Three of the four commentaries answer that question, and those three answer it the same way.

Al-Tabari: until the messengers despaired *of their people believing in Allah and accepting them as truthful in what they brought from Him*. Al-Muyassar: until they despaired *of their people's belief*. Ibn Kathir reports the same from Sa'id b. Jubayr, from Ibn Mas'ud through Tamim b. Hadhlam, and from Mujahid.

Al-Jalalayn does not answer it. It glosses **istay'asa** with the bare synonym **ya'isa**, "gave up hope," and never says what the hope had been in. It moves straight past that to the clause after it — which is where the disagreement actually sits.
edits.evidence: Each edition checked individually in the fetched report. al-Tabari 12:110: "﴿حتى إذا استيأسَ الرسل﴾ ، الذين أرسلناهم إليهم منهم أن يؤمنوا بالله ... ويصدِّقوهم فيما أتوهم به من عند الله" — object supplied. al-Muyassar 12:110: "حتى إذا يئس الرسل من إيمان قومهم" — object supplied. Ibn Kathir 12:110 supplies it from all three named authorities: Sa'id bin Jubayr ("when the Messengers gave up hope that their people will believe in them"); Ibn Mas'ud via Tamim bin Hadhlam ("Tamim bin Hadhlam said, 'I heard 'Abdullah bin Mas'ud comment on this Ayah ... (until, when the Messengers gave up hope) that their people will believe in them'"); Mujahid ("This is also the Tafsir that Mujahid bin Jabr and several other Salaf scholars gave for this Ayah"). al-Jalalayn 12:110, fetched COMPLETE (its entry runs through "﴿عَنِ القَوْم المُجْرِمِينَ﴾ المُشْرِكِينَ" at the end of the verse, so this is not truncation): its only gloss on the verb is "﴿اسْتَيْأَسَ﴾ يَئِسَ ﴿الرُّسُل﴾" — a bare synonym with no object. It then jumps to the zann clause and splits it by recitation.

edits.defect: The 'A'ishah report is real and correctly attributed to Bukhari, but the section misstated WHAT she rejected (given as 'prophets could despair of their Lord's help'), converting a live qira'ah dispute over kudhibu/kudhdhibu into a settled lexical gap and suppressing the ikhtilaf Ibn Kathir explicitly reports in the same passage.
edits.before:
The despair is directed at the audience, not at God. Ibn Kathir preserves 'A'ishah's reaction, in Bukhari, to the suggestion that prophets could despair of their Lord's help: *maʿādh Allāh* — God forbid. She rejected that reading outright.

Left unspecified, "reached despair" invites a reader to supply the object themselves, and the one most likely to be supplied is the one 'A'ishah refused. Naming it removes the ambiguity: the messengers had run out of hope in the people in front of them, and help arrived at exactly that point.
edits.after:
On the despair itself, then, those three read it as aimed at the audience. The clause that comes next is where the commentators actually divide, and the division begins with how one word is recited. **Kudhibu** can be read light (*takhfif*) or with a doubled consonant (*tashdid*), and the two readings send the sentence in different directions. Ibn Kathir says so outright: "there is another way of reciting this word, and there is a difference of opinion about its meaning."

Al-Jalalayn sets the two side by side. With the *tashdid*: the messengers became certain that their people had denied them with a denial after which no faith would follow. With the *takhfif*: the nations thought the messengers had been failed in the victory they were promised.

This is where 'A'ishah's answer belongs, and it is worth reporting exactly. Ibn Kathir carries it from Bukhari: 'Urwah ibn az-Zubayr asked her about this verse, and when he put to her the reading in which the messengers themselves thought the promise made to them had proved false, she answered *maʿādh Allāh* — God forbid — "the Messengers did not suspect their Lord of such a thing." She recited the *tashdid* herself, and she read the clause of the messengers' own followers: the trial ran long, help was delayed, and the messengers came to fear that even those who had believed had gone back on them. So what she rejected was not that the despair had an object. It was one particular way of reading the clause that follows it.

Others read it otherwise, and Ibn Kathir names the split rather than passing over it: some referred that thought to the believing followers, and some to the disbelievers of the nation — in which case the sense becomes that the deniers thought the messengers had been given no true promise of victory. Al-Tabari gathers dozens of these reports, states which recitation he prefers and why, and records 'A'ishah's objection alongside it. This reflection does not settle any of that. The tradition did not settle it quickly either, and the question touches what may and may not be said about prophets, which is not something a tadabbur decides. For that, ask a qualified scholar.

What survives all of it is the shape of the moment. Left unspecified, "reached despair" invites a reader to supply the object themselves, and the one most likely to be supplied is the one 'A'ishah refused. The three commentaries that do specify it point the same way: the messengers had run out of hope in the people in front of them, and help arrived at exactly that point.
edits.evidence: Ibn Kathir 12:110 (fetched): "As for saying of Allah, كُذِبُوا (they were denied) There are two recitations for it. One of them is with a Shadda (meaning: they were betrayed by their people). And this is the way 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, recited it." — the two recitations, and 'A'ishah's own tashdid. Bukhari attribution verified verbatim: "Al-Bukhari said that 'Urwah bin Az-Zubayr narrated that he asked 'Aishah about the meaning of the following verse"; her answer: "A'ishah said, 'Allah forbid! The Messengers did not suspect their Lord of such a thing.'" Her own reading of the verse, in the same report: "This Verse is concerned with the Messengers' followers who had faith in their Lord and believed in their Messengers. The period of trials for those followers was long and Allah's help was delayed until the Messengers gave up hope for the conversion of the disbelievers amongst their nation and suspected that even their followers were shaken in their belief, Allah's help then came to them." The ikhtilaf, named by Ibn Kathir in the same passage: "Therefore, there is another way of reciting this word, and there is a difference of opinion about its meaning." and "some scholars said that the Ayah, وَظَنُّوا أَنَّهُمْ قَدْ كُذِبُوا (and thought that they were denied), is in reference to the believers who followed the Messengers, while some said it is in reference to the disbelievers among the Messengers' nation. In the latter case, the meaning becomes: 'and the disbelievers thought that the Messengers were not given a true promise of victory.'" What 'A'ishah was answering, per the immediately preceding report in Ibn Kathir, is Ibn 'Abbas's light reading ("Then Ibn 'Abbas said to me that they were humans"), which al-Tabari states as "وظنَّتِ الرسل أنهم قد كُذِبوا فيما وُعِدُوا من النصر" — the messengers thought they had been lied to concerning the victory they were promised — hence the wording 'the promise made to them had proved false' rather than the sharper gloss. al-Tabari also carries her words directly: "معاذ الله، لم تكن الرُّسل تظُنُّ بربها ... إنما هم أتباع الرُّسُل" and "فكانت تقرؤها: 'قَدْ كُذِّبُوا'، تثقلها", notes his own preference ("والقراءة على هذا التأويل الذي ذكرنا في قوله: ﴿كُذِبُوا﴾ بضم الكاف وتخفيف الذال") and his reason for rejecting the messengers-referent reading ("وخلافه من القول أشبه بصفات الأنبياء"). al-Jalalayn 12:110 splits the same clause by recitation: "﴿أنَّهُمْ قَدْ كُذِّبُوا﴾ بِالتَّشْدِيدِ تَكْذِيبًا لا إيمان بَعْده والتَّخْفِيف أيْ ظَنَّ الأُمَم أنَّ الرُّسُل أُخْلِفُوا ما وُعِدُوا بِهِ مِن النَّصْر".
